AOnp AnnuaL Report. 


BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


April 30th closed the 42nd year’s history of the Association. We 
gladly recognize those with us who have followed this work for 
young men with active service, and continued friendship and 
sympathy during all these years. 

The total number of visits made to the building last year by young 
men was 183,595, making the daily average 503. We report with 
pleasure an increasing use of the building by the members. Self- 
respecting young men who are non-members are equally and always 
welcome, and we are glad to note that an increasing number of this 
class soon find it in their interests to apply for membership. 

We can confidently report that the ‘‘ Home-life ” of the Association 
is stronger than ever before. This is a most important feature, 
especially when it is remembered that the membership is composed 
of all classes of young men from such a variety of occupations. To 
make the building a ‘‘ Christian Home” for young men who are 
away from home is the aim of the directors. 


FINANCE. 


The financing of this largely increased work has required much 
time and effort. The Association is greatly indebted to its faithful 
treasurer, Mr. Warden King, for his untiring efforts, and also to 
the Finance Committee. Through their exertions, and the personal 
generosity of members of the Board, and friends of the work, the 
amount has been secured for the payment of all the bills for current 
expenses. ‘l’o prevent this heavy strain upon the Finance Committee, 
we would suggest (1st) that the number of the committee be increased. 


8 


znd That many of the contributors be asked to increase their 
subscriptions. In a number of instances the amount given now Is 
the same as when the work was more limited. 3rd. That more of 
our ordinary members who enjoy the privileges of the Association be 
asked to become contributors. The merbership fee is so small com- 
pared with the privileges offered, that it seems within the reach of 
most of the members to make some additional contribution towards 
the Current Expense Fund during the year. This would lessen the 
burden of the Committee, and increase the interest of the members. 
The faithful service rendered by Mr. T. Duncan Patton, who has had 
charge of the financial details, must not be forgotten. In addition 
to this finance work, he has been an efficient Assistant Secretary, ever 
working in the interests of the Association as a whole. 


RELIGIOUS WORK. 


The number of religious meetings and sessions of Bible and 
Training Classes have been 343, with a total attendance of 19,873 
young men. This department is of paramount importance, but it is 
impossible to estimate by the above figures the religious work of the 
building. No single week has passed during the year without seeing 
one or more young men coming as earnest enquirers after a personal 
Saviour. In addition to the regular religious meetings, the corres- 
pondence, the employment, the office work, the reception committee, 
the physical, and in fact, every department is actively used in pressing 
the question of questions as to eternal life. We have a diffidence in 
reporting the number of conversions, as it often takes time and 
patient effort for these results to be fully apparent to us. The direct 
result upon the life of the young man so influenced is but one issue. 
A no less important one is the training which young men receive in 
Bible study and Christian work. This is of the greatest importance. 
At least 150 young men are being trained through these agencies to 
feel their personal responsibility for the salvation of their fellows. 
The system of personal work now adopted is:to make one member 
responsible for some other young man. This responsibility is not 
the result of the enthusiasm of a bright religious service, but the 
development of the ‘‘I am my brother’s keeper” spirit, and therefore 


9 


responsible for agressive effort on his i rant in the workshop, in the 
boarding house, as well as in the religious meeting. To illustrate, 
one member is dressing beside another in the locker room. The 
conversation is turned to personal Christian life. The secretary is told 
of the “open door” in the member’s life, and through the efforts of 
another worker this young man becomes a decided Christian. Like 
hundreds of others he was only waiting for some one to guide 
him. Another member timidly ventured the remark to a fellow- 
clerk whose feet were slipping: “Jim, if you had only joined the 
Association when you first came to the City things might be 
different with you now. They are with me.” It was only a word, but. 
the next day his companion said: ‘I’ve been thinking of what you 
said. You're right, and I’d like to go now if it wasn’t too late, but 
I’m ashamed.” They came, and until he left the City, he was a 
regular attendant at the meetings and Bible Classes. Although in 3 — 
years previous residence in the City he had never attended a church 
service, except on a funeral occasion. Another young man said to a 
fellow-workman who had lost some time through the drink-habit,— 
‘‘T was once as foolish as you are, but look at the change zow. 
Come to Association and sign the pledge.” He did, and through the 
power of Jesus Christ he is a free man from this enemy, and now a 
faithful church member. And so the list might go on, but let these 
suffice to show that it is now, and will be increasingly the aim of the 
Board to develop a class of men who feel a definite responsibility 
for seeking to influence the lives of the young men they touch in 
business and social life, and who are being trained in practical 
methods of doing it. The Religious Work committee should provide 
for at least two series of evangelistic meetings for young men—one 
in Vovember, another in Aprz/—under the guidance of a qualified 
evangelist. This has been a defect in the past year’s work. It was 
tried, but the leader could not be secured. 


MEMBERSHIP. 


637 new members have been added during the year, making the 
total number of paid-up members on April 30th, 1684. By our 
present system no man’s name is continued on the roll unless he has 


10 


paid his fee in advance. The first year in a new building always 
places the membership about 20 / larger than it will be ordinarily. 
The past year, therefore, gives us a fair test, and through the efforts 
of our members, and the privileges offered, we expect to see a 
gradual increase each year. The Finance Committee’s estimate 
from members’ fees was $5,000. This has been exceeded by $262. 
Good effective work can be done by the Association, as men are 
retained year by year, and this question should receive the earnest 
consideration of the Membership Committee. 


EDUCATIONAL. 


During the year, 440 students were enrolled in the evening 
classes, and instruction was given in twelve branches. ‘This 


‘evening class work has come to be a fundamental plank in the 


platform of the Association history of this country, and the Associa- 
tion which neglects this misses its opportunity, By this means an 
increasing number of the mechanical young men will be reached and 
held in the work. Habits of systematic study are formed, which will 
mould character and qualify for true citizenship. A class in manual 
training should be added as soon as possible. When so much 
interest is being taken in educational work in this City, we urge 
the claims of this most important class, viz. those who are eager 
to add to their limited education by the wise use of evening 
hours. 

A Current Topic Club is a necessary addition to our educational 
work. Besides the training in public speech which it would afford, 
the reading of many members would be directed so as to secure for 
them an intelligent review of the important questions of the day. 
Let this be an additional feature for next October. 


PHYSICAL. 


This department is just passing its formative stage, and is now 
being planned upon a system of graded classes, which will lead to 
progressive work and the best general development of the body, 
while it affords the attractive pleasure which is now so increasingly 


11 


popular, of physical recreation, Under the careful supervision of Mr. 
W. H. Ball, our competent physical director, at least, 1,000 men have 
taken advantage of the benefits of this department, full particulars of 
which will be found in their report. 


SOCIAL. 


The Reception Hall in our building is a special social feature in 
itself. But this requires to be seconded by living voices, faces and 
sympathetic interest. The secretaries during the day and members 
of the Reception Committee in the evenings have furnished this 
supply. But much more can and should be done. The first 
impression a young man receives so often decides his future interest, 
that his reception becomes a matter of vital importance to the 
Association. Therefore every member should charge himself with 
this duty when in the building, and when the Opportunity occurs. 
A defect in our social work is in the introduction of new members. 
Some plan must be devised by the committee which will bring the 
secretaries and the older members in contact with the new men as 
they join each month, which will make them feel “ at home” from 
the start. 

The introduction of the game of chess every Tuesday and 
Thursday evenings in the Parlor has been an excellent feature. 
Through the co-operation of several members this has been Started, 
and quite a number are becoming enthusiastic players. 


LIBRARY. 


The importance of this invaluable adjunct to the work has not 
been fully realized. We are now waking up. The aim should be 
(1st) a qualified librarian to care for the books and wisely direct the 
reading of members, and (znd) 10,000 selected volumes on the 
shelves. The committee’s report shows what has been accomplished. 
Here is an excellent opportunity for a permanent investment, which 
opens to the wealthy and prosperous citizen a field for broad 
philanthropy and noble Christian endeavour. 


JUNIOR WORK. 


This department has a growing interest, and demands the wisest 
supervision. Here we must look for our best trained workers. We 
see them now on our committees, in the college work, and taking 
active part in other cities. ‘Through this work we connect ourselves 
more closely with the homes of the City, and secure the sympathy and 
co-operation of the parents. The report to be read shows the past 
year’s record to have been the most fruitful one in the history of the 
department. The plan of work is well defined, and is now frequently 
quoted by the other Associations as one of the best and most 
practical methods of Boys’ Work. ' 

It is with regret that we have to announce the resignation of Mr. 
D. W. Corbett, as assistant secretary, having in charge this depart- 
ment. He has accepted the position as secretary of the Honolulu 
Association, and leaves here on the z9th. Since his conversion, seven 
years ago, he has been actively identified with the work, and God 
has used him in winning many into the Christian life. This has been 
especially true amongst the boys, so that in going to his far distant 
field, he will carry the personal affection of many who have passed 
from death unto life through his friendship and ministry. While we 
all join in the prayer that God’s blessing may rest upon his life and 
service, we would not forget to call upon our members to pray the 
Lord of the Harvest that He could thrust out other labourers into 
His Harvest field. 

BRANCHES. 

Again we regret that we cannot report the establishment of two 
much needed branches. Why? Not because these sections of the 
City are not ready, nor for lack of men to direct the work, but for 
lack of funds for this purpose. The pastors and churches are calling 
for them ; saloons and places of evil resort are increasing in these 
sections, and the young men are greatly in need of this preventive 
agency, and would gladly support it had they the opportunity. What 


“the Directors need is a 


SPECIAL FUND. 


for the extension of the work in the City. No central building can 
possibly reach the young men in these sections. New York has this 


13 


work carried on at ten points in their City, under one Managing 
Board ; Brooklyn, Chicago, Pittsburg, Philadelphia, have the same. 
Toronto has two branches. A healthy work for the young men of 
any City must grow. But the Board appreciates the danger of 
extension without a permanent Fund to establish the work and assist 
in meeting its yearly needs. Knowing the needs of the City, we 
present the facts to our fellow-citizens, and continue our prayer to 
God to supply this need, so that the lives of many more of our young 
men and youths may be saved from inevitable ruin, into which so 


many fall. 
EXTENSION FUND. 


9 


This education on the line of ‘‘ systematic giving’’ to extend the 
work at home and abroad has continued. 51 contributors by 

| envelope system, from 5 cents to 20 cents per week have given $335.08 

' and special gifts have been made to the work in India, to the 
amount of $500.00. One result of this line of work has been that 

one of our directors has assumed the expense of sending Mr. J. 
Campbell White to India as a worker amongst young men in 
Calcutta. He sails in August, and his reports will doubtless stir up 


our workers here. 
DEATHS 


During the year we have lost by death, Thos. O’Brien, H. R. 
Ransom, J. A. Milligan, H. O. Wilson, Geo. S. Lovejoy, J. H. M. 
Welch, W. D. Davidson, all active members. (R. C. Lyman died 
February 1892.) 

From our list of subscribers who have supported the work for 
many years, we have to record the following: John Duncan, Dr. 
Geo. Ross, W. C. Munderloh, Mr. D. Fraser. 

This list is a loud call to our members for added service in this 
our time of opportunity. 


A CLOSING WORD. 


We have tried to pervade every section of the work with the 
spirit of Christ. He came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, 
and members have been encouraged to personal self-sacrifice for the 
benefit of their fellows. Many have found, in self-sacrifice, their 


14 


highest pleasure, for it is ever more blessed to give than to receive, 
To have the privilege of counselling personally with those who are 
entering the Christian life is a great joy. Oh that more of our 
members had shared it. But the record of the year is closed ; as it 
is the most delightful service in which one can engage, we hope this 
year will find a larger number eager to buy these golden opportunities, 
whereby a life is often saved for time, and a soul for eternity, and 
the result of which will surely be to hear the Master say: ‘‘ Inasmuch 
as ye did it to one of these, ye did it to me.” We regret so little. 
has been accomplished, but here is an opportunity to enter into 
sympathetic and helpful relations with hundreds of young men. 
Fellow members, it is our privilege to lead amongst the young men 
of the City, a life, in spirit and thought, like the young man of 
Nazareth who has left us an example that we should follow in His 
steps. 


Secretary.

MONTREAL, July 1oth, 1893. 


To the President and Direetors of the Young Men’s Christian Association: ‘ 
GENTLEMEN,—We beg to report having audited the Books of the Association a 
for the year ending 30th April, 1893, and to have found them correct and satis. __ 
factory, and have certified the statements presented as being correctly drawn from — 
them. | Respectfully submitted, 
F.. S. BOSS:& SONS, 
Chartered Accountants.

those as members who have actually paid their fee in advance. In former years 
this was not done and many names were carried forward in the hope of securing 
their renewal. On April 30th, the roll stands as follows :—

YOUNG MEN’S MEETINGS. 


During the year the usual meeting’s have been held every Saturday evening 
with good results. This is essentially the Young Men’s Meeting and the speakers, 
for the most part, young men. 

52 meetings in all have been held, with a total attendance of 3,556, making 
an average of 68, a slight increase over the previous year. This is gratifying, 
but our hall will seat 150 and should be filled. Who will help us to fill it ? 

Although the attendance has not been as large as hoped for, the results have 
been most satisfactory. Many young men have come into the light directly 
through this meeting, some of whom are now trying to bring their associates. 
Others, again, have been greatly helped in their Christian life. At the close of 
every meeting an opportunity is given, to any who wish to commence the new 
life, to manifest such a desire, and it is a source of much gratification to see the 
large numbers who ask an interest in the prayers of the meeting. 

Our thanks are especially due to the gentlemen who so efficiently presided at 
the organ and piano and led the singing during the year. 

We close our report with an appeal to our members. Young men who 
crowd the floor of the gymnasium six nights of the week. Let this be personal. 
Can you not spare one night for the Young Men’s Meetings. Especially do we 
appeal to our active members who work in the gymnasium to consider the matter. 

Our motto for the past year has been, in the words of the Master, ‘‘ Lo, I am 
with you!” In his strength we go forward. 

W. M. McCUNN, 


Secretary. 


MEN’S MEETING. 


The past year has been largely experimental in connection with the Men’s 
Meeting, Sunday afternoon. The object of the meeting has been to win young 
men who are not attracted by a Bible Class and spend the afternoon on the 
street. To this end, the chief feature is an address, by some able speaker, dealing 
with some subject of practical value to young men: not only has an effort been 
made to secure popular speakers, but to so vary the subjects that something new 
would be presented each week. Four meetings were addressed by lawyers, three 
by doctors, others by business men and clergymen. To the last-mentioned we 
are certainly much indebted, for, though Sunday is the busiest day of the week 
for them, they have always willingly responded to our calls. 

The Association Orchestra has been of invaluable assistance in EN the 
meetings attractive, as have, also, Mr. S. S. Bain and other singers. 

Whenever possible, visitors in the City have been secured. Among these we 
note :—Rev. Jas. Cook, D.D., of Boston; late Chas. P. Wills, Esq. (Vice- 
President Brotherhood of St. Andrew), New York; Bishop Baldwin, of Huron ; 
Mr. Alex. Gustafson, New York; Mr. W. B. Wookey, London; Mr. L. D. 
Wishard, New York; Mr. J. W. Bengough, Toronto; Rev. Mr. Stevens, of 
China; Mr. J. Campbell White, Secretary-elect to China, and Dr. Seerley, of 
Springfield. 


24 


Beginning June 19th, with 4o present, the attendance has gradually increased 

—several times filling Association Hall—until the record shows an average of 
174. : 
Our first aim being to build up a meeting, the definite results have not been 
as large as we trust they will be in the future. Our encouragement has been in 
seeing men listening with rapt attention to vigorous presentations of the Gospel— 
men, too, who do not, as a rule, attend other meetings in the Association. The 
precious seed has been sown in many hearts, and we doubt not but that the 
harvest will come in due time. 


JAMES WILSON, 


Chairman. 


YOUNG MEN’S BIBLE STUDY. 


The year just past has been the most successful in the history of this class, 
Not alone in point of attendance—which has averaged 83—has this success been 
apparent, but in definite practical results. Hardly a week has passed without 
one or more young men enquiring the way of salvation. 

While your Committee has been greatly encouraged, we are not satisfied—nor 
can we be until the class-room is full to overflowing. Plans are now being 
laid to more thoroughly canvas the boarding-houses of this city, and secure the 
young men who live there. 

The thanks of the Committee are hereby tendered to Mr. W. T. Walmsley 
for his faithful services as organist, also to the friends who so ably conducted the 
class in the absence of Mr. Budge. 


Respectfully submitted, 


FRANK P. RITCHIE, 
Chairman. 


INVITATION COMMITTEE. 


As in other years, so during the past the Invitation Committee has endeavoured, 
through the distribution of printed slips on the streets, to invite men to the Gospel 
meetings. A large number of special invitations were issued last year announcing 
speakers and subjects, packages of these being mailed to active members of the 
Association in shops and offices. This has brought the Association, through its 
members, into personal touch with young men, and has been effective in drawing 
many to the building. 

Our difficulty has been to secure enough workers to effectually carry on this 
work Saturday evenings. It is work that requires very little time, though regular 
attendance is essential. We can always place new workers, and will be glad to 
receive such. 

Sunday afternoon work has been more satisfactory, and has resulted in many 
attending the Men’s meeting. 

In all, 38,000 cards were distributed during the year, showing that some effort 


was made to direct men into the right way. 
"BR. Je WILLIAMS; 


Chatrman. 


25 


EXTENSION COMMITTEE. 


‘¢ Extension” is the Association name for the home and foreign missionary 
department. Trained missionary Secretaries are now found in the following 
foreign fields, viz., India, Japan, Brazil and Mexico—all of whom work under the 
supervision of the International Committee. 

This work of the Extension Committee should exist if only for the education 
in Christian stewardship which it affords to those who by it are forming the habit 
in life of laying aside systematically a portion of their substance for God’s work. 
Addresses before the Association in this work have been given by Messrs. S. A. 
Taggart, L. D. Wishard, J. R. Mott and J. Campbell White of the International 
Committee, and Mr. C. F. Falconer, of Ottawa, which were all highly instructive. 
To enforce its work still further upon the attention of the Association, frequent 
articles were contributed by Mr. Corbett to the ‘‘ Record.” At present there are 
51 active contributors by envelopes, whose annual subscriptions amount to $335.08. 
Of this amount 27 seniors contribute $257.60 by subscriptions ranging from 5 to 
50 cents weekly, and 24 juniors $77.48 by subcriptions of from 2 to 25 cents 
weekly. 

As this report closes the first five years of the history of this fund, a short 
statement of the work done will be of interest.

EDUCATIONAL REPORT. 


The oan of the Educational Department of the Montreal Young Men’s 
Christian Association has now extended over a period of nearly twenty years, and 
during this time has been marked by a steady growth. The method of work has 
been eminently practical ; its aim has been to teach those branches that will 
help a young man in the business or trade in which he is employed. It meets 
an urgent and recognized need with a large class of young men, who, being 
employed during the day, wish to spend their evenings in such a manner as will 
improve their future opportunities for advancement in life. 

The Session of ’92-3 was opened by a gathering, on the 29th of September, 
which was well attended, and at which a very enjoyable address was presented by 
Prof. John Cox, of McGill University. The closing exercises were held on 
Thursday evening, the 13th April. About two hundred students and their friends 


"were then assembled in the small Lecture. Room, which was tastefully decorated, 


27 


and the walls of the room hung with specimens of the students’ work. The 
programme for the evening was an exhibition and illustration on the part of each 
class and its instructor of the work accomplished during the winter. The first 
item on the programme was given by the orchestra. It showed the careful work 
of this body during the winter, and of its leader, Prof. Hume. Mr. Charles T, 
Bale then gave the assembly an idea of what could be accomplished during a 
winter’s term in the study of Shorthand. One of the pupils wrote to dictation, 
on a blackboard, from an extract from an evening paper, which was afterwards 
translated by other pupils. Several of Mr. Bale’s pupils had acquired the speed 
of 80 to 100 words per minute during the winter’s course. The most notable 
progress in Educational Class work during the past Session, has been that of 
the Drawing Class, under the instruction of Mr. Henry Seymour. Pupils in 
Mechanical and Architectural Drawing, and other work demanding the use of 
mathematical instruments, took an elementary course in plain Geometry before 
taking up the course they particularly desired. Excellent progress was also 
afterwards shown in Freehand and Model Drawing. In this connection it is 
desired to express thanks to Messrs. Laurie Bros., for a box in which to keep 
apparatus, generously given the class, also to Mr. McArthur, for the loan of cast 
models, and to the Instructor, for much of the material needed. Mr. I. Gammell, 
of the Commercial Arithmetic Class, then gave an exhibition of training in 
Mental Arithmetic, which showed good progress in this line, The same teacher 
had charge of the work in English Composition, which class, though small, has 
done good work. eports of the work in Book-keeping and Penmanship were 
given by the teacher, Mr. Bannell Sawyer, who has now had charge of the work 
for two Sessions. 

The Chatauqua Class gave an example of an evening at work, which proved 
very entertaining ; Mr. C. T. Williams, the instructor, having the happy faculty 
of showing forth such a class to advantage. About twenty members of the 
Vocal Music Class, under the direction of Mr. Herbert Patton, entertained the 
audience with one of their popular glees, which showed the training they had 
been subjected to during the year. ) ; 

This closing evening was declared by all a decided success. It is understood 
that some of the class exhibits will be forwarded to the Indianapolis Convention, 
and, possibly, to the Y.M.C.A. exhibit at the ‘‘ World’s Fair.”” As a number 
of the students were very unwilling to give up their work, several of the classes 
purpose continuing their sessions during the coming summer. 

A new feature, which was taken up by the Educational Class Committee 
during the Winter Session of ’92-3, was a course of lectures following out the 
University Extension idea. Twelve lectures were given by Prof. John Cox, of 
McGill, entitled ‘*‘ Energy in Nature: an Introduction to Physical Science.” 
131 students enrolled in this class, and the average attendance was over I00. 
Through the courtesy of the McGill Faculty, several of the lectures were held 
in the new science building, in order that the lecturer might have the use of the 
instruments belonging to the College. The only regrettable feature was that so 
few students in this class came up for the final examinations; all who did so, 
however, passed with credit, and a certificate is to be issued to all such. 


28 


The following students were recommended for distinction by their teachers :— 
French, Elementary.—John Duthie, J. R. Adam, T. G. Donnelly. 
« Advanced.—W. A. Roy, F. L. Jermyn, W. Webb.

MEMBERS’ MEETING AND ENTERTAINMENT 
COMMITTEE. 


Perhaps no Committee in connection with the Association has felt to a greater 
extent the advantages incident to the occupancy of the New Building, and the 
increased facilities therein provided for the proper carrying out of its work, than 
has the Members’ Meeting and Entertainment Committee. Social meetings have 
been held each month, at which the ladies of different Churches kindly assisted. 
The New Year’s Reception proved most successful, the Building being crowded 
during the entire afternoon and evening. 


29 


For the evening of October 31st, your Committee arranged a new feature of 
the Social work in the shape of a “ Fireside Talk,’’ which was held in the 
Reception Hall,—Members surrounding the open grate fire to tell stories, sing 
songs, and dispose of taffy, apples, nuts, etc. 

In conclusion, your Committee begs to express its sincere thanks to the ladies 
and gentlemen who so kindly contributed to the success of the meetings arranged | 
by it. G. A. IRWIN, 

Chairman. 


RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 

There are few more important Committees than the Evening Reception 
Committee in connection with the Association, or that call for more faithful 
effort on the part of its representative members, and while during the past year 
it is felt that at times the work of the Committee has not been as it might have 
been, still it is hoped that the labor has not been in vain. Some of the members 
are inexperiened in the work and while willing are easily discouraged, others are 
careless in attendance, and too often the work of the Committee falls on a minority 
of its members. 

The following statistics may give some idea of the work that is being done— 
results cannot be measured. 

During the year there have been 12 Committee Meetings held with an average 
attendance of about Io. 

The Evening Reception work has been carried on during 268 evenings by 
460 members. The rooms are usually, where practicable, closed with prayers, a 
record kept of 173 evenings showing an attendance of 1,318—an average of a little 
under eight. 

It is with a sense of shortcoming in some of the most essential points of our 
work that this report is made up, and it is hoped that both the old and new 
members of the Committee will, in the ensuing year, come resolved to do their 
work faithfully and in that esprit de corps which during the past year has been 
lacking. 

Let each feel that personal responsibility and be faithful and ready servants in 
this part of the Master’s vineyard. GEO. W. JONES, 

Chairman. 


REPORT OF PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


Your Committee begs to report as follows :—- 

The year just ended has been the first full year for this department, (1891-2 
having been only a broken year) and therefore a fair test of the usefulness and 
popularity of this department of the work. It has been an exceedingly busy year 
(21 classes having been held each week) and, we believe, lasting benefits have 
been conferred on the membership, not only in improved health and physique, as 
shown by the examinations, but also, by the healthy spiritual tone, and the good 
example of the Christian athlete, whether seen on the Gymnasium Floor or on the 
field. Mr. Ball has continued with us, as Physical Director, and to his wisdom 
and enthusiasm are the good results largely due. 


eal | 


0 


oO 


Mr. Powter was appointed his assistant in Nov. 1892, and has proved himself 
in every way a most popular and able coadjutor. The following are the figures 
furnished to the Committee by Mr. Ball :— 

Gymnasium Classes started Sept. 19th, 1892. Average attendance at Boys’ 
Classes has been 39. The number of boys attending the classes has not been as 
large, but the attendance has been very much more regular, than last year. 

Business Men’s Class has had a fair attendance only. 

Pastor's Class ditto. Previous to the grading of the Young Men’s Class, the 
average attendance was 69. Since the grading (Nov. 29th.) the average of the 
Ist Class has been 14, 2nd Class has been 7, 3rd and Preparatory Class has 
been 77. Total is 98 against the previous 69. 

Being the first season of the graded work, and the standard for admission to 
the Ist and 2nd Classes, being high, the total membership in both of these 
Classes has necessarily been small. 

Classes have been held regularly with the exception of three days during the 
Provincial Convention. 

Since May Ist, 1892, 490 young men, 72 boys, total 562, have been examined 
(these are new members). Since starting Nov. 1891, 963 young men, 299 boys ; 
grand total 7262 examinations. 

In addition a large number have availed of the privilege of having themselves 
re-examined. 

The Leaders’ Classes shew a total membership of 21. 

Mr. Kingman has added greatly to the interest and enthusiasm of the 
Gymnasium work by the offer of two gold and two silver medals, competition for 
which is shortly to take place. | 

It is proposed to test the desirability of szmmer work instde, by continuing a 
few of the Classes during the summer, (or a portion of it) to test its popularity. 

Gymnasium Apparatus is reported to be in good condition. Bow/ing Alleys 
were relevelled and improved (vzde special report). Baths; Want of a plentiful 
and regular supply of /o¢ water is still felt, especially for the Plunge Bath, the 
temperature of which is often too low. The rear portion of the Dorchester Street 
store was appropriated for locker space. 262 new lockers were made, although not 
all taken, we would have been overcrowded without them. 


OUT DOOR WORK, 


The Physical Department cannot possibly be kept up to its proper condition, 
without the possession, or at least wzse of Good Grounds. The felt need of grounds 
grows upon us year by year. The ‘‘ Driving Park,” secured last year, was not a 
success, This year, so far, an arrangement has been made to rent the Shamrock 
Grounds for two mornings in the week, but practices for evenings and also for 
Saturday afternoons are almost indispensable. 

The Association is indebted to Dr. Drummond, for his work done as Medical 
Examiner. 

Hlealth Talks were given with great profit to our members, by Dr. W. G. 
Stewart, Dr. Kirkpatrick, and Dr. Drummond, also we were favored with a visit 
from Dr. Seerley, of the Springfield School, whose addresses were most acceptable

The Committee has been able to carry out all this work within the 
appropriation allotted to them. 

Detailed reports from the Snow-Shoe Club, Water Polo, Bowling Alley, and 
other sub-committees in connection with their special games, etc., as also a record

The whole respectfully submitted. D.. W.. ROSS, 

Chairman. 


EMPLOYMENT. 

565 applications for employment have been received and placed on file during the 
past year. For these 197 situations were secured at salaries ranging from $75.00 
to $1200.00 perannum. One of the features of the work has been the large 
number of members making use of the Bureau. 760 letters of introduction to 
various firms were written, and 14 men were enquirers in the Saturday evening 


meetings. D. W. CORBETT. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 

During the year there has been a marked increase among the members in 
Bible Study, and a consequent growth in their spiritual life and work. We have 
also seen a good development in Committee work. The Religious work has 
received the first place, and has been very fruitful, many encouraging results 
having been obtained. We refer directly to the large number who have united 
with their different Churches, 47 in all, and we feel it is largely due to the 
training classes and boys’ meetings that this has been brought about. It has 
been impossible to give an accurate number of inquirers and those who have 
been led to Jesus. Christ, but we know, from the personal testimony of the boys, 
that we can safely put it down at 50 at the least. 

The training classes have proved to be as valuable as ever in the training of 
workers and in the study of the Bible. A marked advance has been seen in the 
membership of. these. 

The Friday meeting is still the centre of the work, and has been blessed. 
It has been held weekly, with but two exceptions. A valuable feeder to this 
meeting has been the Mass. Meeting, held quarterly, from which much good has 
been obtained. 

An increasing interest in Christian giving has been manifested, the Depart- 
ment now contributing through 24 members.to the Extension Fund. 

The Children’s. Ward of the General. Hospital has been visited: one Sunday 
in each month by.the Secretary and a number of the members holding a short 
song-service, and a distribution of papers and good things being made to the 
little sick ones. 

The Social side has had its place and proved a success throughout, each 
gathering held having been well attended and appreciated. A course of four 
illustrated lectures was given and proved helpful. 


o2 


A, steady advance has been made physically. The work done in the 
gymnasium has been very encouraging. A fine exhibition from two classes at the 
closing social, showed how carefully the boys had been trained and the results 
coming from it. The usual Snow-shoe Club added largely to make the out-door 
part successful. 

The Library has been used to its fullest capacity, and no estimate can be 
made of the good done by this means in this day when the books read by a 
large number of boys are of a very bad kind, and have a bad effect upon them. 
The 148 members using this privilege have taken out 4,608 volumes, and, as only 
one book is allowed to be taken out each week, you can form an idea of the good 
reading that has been done. There are only 625 books on our shelves. 

We sorrow and regret the loss we are about to sustain in the removal of our 
Secretary, Mr. Corbett. Our Report would be incomplete did we not speak of 
him and his work among us. He has won the respect and affection of our 
membership and of those who have attended our meetings, and has been used of 
God in leading many of them to Christ. We pray that God may richly bless 
him in his new work, and use him to be a blessing to those he goes to labour 
among. He will take away from us, not only our prayers, but our warmest 
sympathy and love. 

There have been many kind friends who have helped us in many ways, and 
especially those who have donated pictures, books, ete. We would now take this 
opportunity of thanking them. We may say we are still open for anything in 
this way.
